title: Linear Models and Intro to Deep Learning

questions.question: What is the key difference between maximum likelihood (ML) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation?

options.text: MAP uses a prior over parameters, while ML does not.
options.explanation: MAP explicitly incorporates a prior distribution p(θ) to combine prior knowledge with the data, whereas ML maximizes only the likelihood p(D|θ) and effectively assumes a uniform prior.

options.text: MAP is used only for classification tasks, while ML is for regression.
options.explanation: Both ML and MAP can be applied to any modeling problem (regression or classification); the distinction is not task-specific but lies in whether a prior is used.

options.text: MAP requires computing the model evidence, while ML ignores it.
options.explanation: Neither ML nor MAP requires the evidence term p(D); MAP uses the prior and likelihood product, while ML uses only the likelihood. The evidence is needed for the full posterior predictive distribution.

options.text: MAP always yields more accurate predictions than ML.
options.explanation: MAP can outperform ML when the prior is informative, but it is not universally better—it may bias results if the prior is misspecified. ML is a special case of MAP with a flat prior.

questions.question: Using L2 weight decay (ridge regression) in a linear model corresponds to assuming which prior on the weights?

options.text: A Gaussian prior centered at zero
options.explanation: The L2 penalty term λ||w||² in the objective is exactly the negative log of a Gaussian prior with zero mean and precision proportional to λ, making the MAP solution equivalent to ridge regression.

options.text: A Laplace prior centered at zero
options.explanation: A Laplace prior leads to an L1 penalty (LASSO), not L2. The choice of prior governs the type of regularization.

options.text: A uniform prior over a bounded interval
options.explanation: A uniform prior does not penalize large weights and would correspond to no regularization (maximum likelihood) within the interval.

options.text: No prior (pure maximum likelihood)
options.explanation: Omitting the prior corresponds to maximum likelihood estimation, which has no regularization term. Ridge regression explicitly includes a prior that shrinks weights toward zero.

questions.question: What loss function does binary logistic regression minimize when using maximum likelihood?

options.text: The squared error loss
options.explanation: Squared error is derived from a Gaussian noise assumption and is typical for linear regression, not for classification with binary targets.

options.text: The cross-entropy loss
options.explanation: Maximizing the Bernoulli likelihood leads directly to the cross-entropy error −∑[t ln y + (1−t) ln(1−y)], which measures the divergence between predicted probabilities and true labels.

options.text: The hinge loss function
options.explanation: Hinge loss is used in support vector machines, not in logistic regression. It does not arise from a probabilistic likelihood.

options.text: The exponential loss function
options.explanation: Exponential loss is used in boosting algorithms like AdaBoost; it is not the negative log-likelihood for logistic regression.

questions.question: Why is gradient descent the standard method for training logistic regression models?

options.text: There is no closed-form solution for this problem
options.explanation: The negative log-likelihood of logistic regression does not have an analytical minimizer; the normal equations derived from the derivative are nonlinear in w, so iterative optimization like gradient descent is required.

options.text: The closed-form solution is numerically unstable
options.explanation: No closed-form solution exists at all, not even an unstable one. The likelihood equations are transcendental and must be solved iteratively.

options.text: Gradient descent guarantees finding the global minimum
options.explanation: Gradient descent is a local optimization method and provides no guarantee of global optimality, especially in non-convex problems. Logistic regression loss is convex, but the algorithm itself does not guarantee global convergence from any starting point.

options.text: It is faster than solving the normal equations directly
options.explanation: There are no normal equations for logistic regression in the sense of a linear system; the gradient descent update is the only practical approach, not a faster alternative to a nonexistent analytical solution.

questions.question: Why is a nonlinear activation function essential in a feedforward neural network with multiple layers?

options.text: Without nonlinearity, the entire network reduces to a linear model
options.explanation: A composition of linear functions remains linear; without a nonlinear activation between layers, the network can only represent linear mappings, negating the benefit of depth.

options.text: It speeds up the convergence of gradient descent
options.explanation: Nonlinearities can sometimes slow down convergence (e.g., saturating functions) and are not chosen primarily for convergence speed; their role is to enable complex function approximation.

options.text: It prevents the model from overfitting the training data
options.explanation: Nonlinearity increases model capacity, which can actually lead to overfitting; regularization techniques, not activation functions, are used to control overfitting.

options.text: It encourages the weights to be sparse
options.explanation: Sparsity is typically induced by specific regularizers (e.g., L1 penalty) or architectures; activation functions like ReLU can produce sparse activations but do not directly regularize weights toward sparsity.
